claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Niu et al., 2011

claims.claim: LIN-39 maintains its own expression through positive autoregulation.
claims.source: Biochemical studies have indeed identified that LIN-39 binds onto its own cis-regulatory region (Niu et al., 2011), suggesting that it maintains its own expression through positive autoregulation.
claims.evidence: Inferred from LIN-39 binding to its own cis-regulatory region

claims.claim: The expression of egl-5, lin-39, and mab-5 is not affected in unc-3 null mutants.
claims.source: To distinguish between these two possibilities, we first monitored the expression of egl-5, lin-39, and mab-5 fosmid-based reporters in unc-3 null mutants. We did not detect any defects (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated through experimental analysis shown in Figure 5A

claims.claim: The expression of unc-3 is not affected in egl-5 mutants.
claims.source: Conversely, the expression of unc-3 is not affected in egl-5 mutants (Figure 5B), suggesting that unc-3 and Hox proteins may act in parallel pathways that function synergistically to control MN subclass-specific gene expression.
claims.evidence: Demonstrated through experimental analysis shown in Figure 5B

claims.claim: unc-3 and Hox proteins may act in parallel pathways that function synergistically to control motor neuron subclass-specific gene expression.
claims.source: Conversely, the expression of unc-3 is not affected in egl-5 mutants (Figure 5B), suggesting that unc-3 and Hox proteins may act in parallel pathways that function synergistically to control MN subclass-specific gene expression.
claims.evidence: Inferred from lack of cross-regulatory interactions

claims.claim: Hox genes do not affect the expression of ACh pathway genes (VAChT, ChAT, ChT).
claims.source: The notion of independence is further supported by the lack of an effect of Hox genes on the expression of ACh pathway genes (VAChT, ChAT, ChT), which are direct UNC-3 target genes in all MNs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated through experimental analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claims.claim: ACh pathway genes (VAChT, ChAT, ChT) are direct UNC-3 target genes in all motor neurons.
claims.source: The notion of independence is further supported by the lack of an effect of Hox genes on the expression of ACh pathway genes (VAChT, ChAT, ChT), which are direct UNC-3 target genes in all MNs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: Based on established knowledge from previous studies

claims.claim: unc-3(fp8); lin-39 mab-5 triple mutants display a more severe effect on unc-129 and del-1 expression compared to lin-39 mab-5 double or unc-3(fp8) single mutants.
claims.source: We find that unc-3(fp8); lin-39 mab-5 triple mutants display a more severe effect on unc-129 and del-1 expression when compared to lin-39 mab-5 double or unc-3(fp8) single mutants (Figure 5C–D).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated through experimental analysis shown in Figure 5C–D

claims.claim: UNC-3 and Hox factors act synergistically to generate DA and VA subclass diversity.
claims.source: To sum up, the stronger effects on unc-129 and del-1 expression in unc-3(fp8); lin-39 mab-5 triple mutants together with the absence of cross-regulatory interactions between UNC-3 and Hox lead us to conclude that these regulatory factors act synergistically to generate DA and VA subclass diversity by controlling the expression of subclass-specific genes.
claims.evidence: Inferred from genetic analysis showing additive effects in triple mutants

claims.claim: The GATTGATG sequence is a putative binding site for LIN-39 in C. elegans cells.
claims.source: Despite lacking cell-type specificity, these ChIP-seq studies have identified the GATTGATG sequence as a putative binding site for LIN-39 in C. elegans cells (Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: Based on ChIP-seq data from modENCODE project

claims.claim: Copies of the LIN-39 motif and COE motif are present in minimal cis-regulatory elements of unc-129 and del-1.
claims.source: Focusing on two of the subclass-specific markers, unc-129 and del-1, we found copies of this LIN-39 motif (as well as copies of the UNC-3 binding site, termed COE motif) in minimal cis-regulatory elements (243 bp for unc-129 and 488 bp for del-1) that drive reporter gene expression in DA1-7/DB and VA1-11/VB MNs, respectively (Figure 6B,E).
claims.evidence: Based on bioinformatic analysis and cis-regulatory analysis shown in Figure 6B,E

claims.claim: Mutation of LIN-39 sites in the unc-129 element results in dramatic loss of reporter gene expression in DA1-7 and DB neurons.
claims.source: To test the functionality of the putative LIN-39 sites (GATTGATG), we mutated these sites in the unc-129 element (243 bp LIN-39 SITES 6 & 7 MUT) and observed a dramatic loss of reporter gene expression in the DA1-7 and DB neurons (Figure 6B–D), which phenocopies the effect observed in lin-39 mab-5 double mutants (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated through mutational analysis shown in Figure 6B–D

claims.claim: ChIP-seq data show adjacent binding for LIN-39 and MAB-5 on the unc-129 243 bp region.
claims.source: ChIP-seq data from the modENCODE consortium show adjacent binding for LIN-39 (as well as MAB-5) on the unc-129_243 bp region that we have defined through our cis-regulatory analysis (Figure 6—figure supplement 1)(Boyle et al., 2014; Niu et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Boyle et al., 2014 and Niu et al., 2011, and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1

claims.claim: Mutation of one LIN-39 site in the del-1 element results in reduction of reporter gene expression in VA1-11 and VB neurons.
claims.source: Moreover, mutation of one LIN-39 site in the del-1 element (488 bp LIN-39 SITE 4 MUT) resulted in a reduction of reporter gene expression in VA1-11 and VB neurons (Figure 6E–F).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated through mutational analysis shown in Figure 6E–F

claims.claim: LIN-39 directly controls expression of the motor neuron subclass-specific genes unc-129 and del-1 through a discrete cis-regulatory motif.
claims.source: Altogether, our findings suggest that, similar to UNC-3, the Hox protein LIN-39 (possibly together with MAB-5) directly controls expression of the MN subclass-specific genes unc-129 and del-1 through a discrete cis-regulatory motif (Figure 5E).
claims.evidence: Inferred from cis-regulatory analysis and mutational studies

claims.claim: In egl-5 mutants, 100% display del-1 de-repression in VA12.
claims.source: We found that 100% of egl-5 mutants display del-1 de-repression in VA12, while in 84.2% of egl-5 mutants unc-129 is de-repressed in DA9 (Figure 7A).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated through experimental analysis shown in Figure 7A

claims.claim: In 84.2% of egl-5 mutants, unc-129 is de-repressed in DA9.
claims.source: We found that 100% of egl-5 mutants display del-1 de-repression in VA12, while in 84.2% of egl-5 mutants unc-129 is de-repressed in DA9 (Figure 7A).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated through experimental analysis shown in Figure 7A

claims.claim: egl-5 promotes posterior motor neuron subclass identity and represses more anterior motor neuron subclass identity.
claims.source: Hence, egl-5 promotes posterior MN subclass identity and represses more anterior MN subclass identity.
claims.evidence: Inferred from de-repression of anterior markers in posterior neurons in egl-5 mutants

claims.claim: Mis-expression of egl-5 in all DA neurons results in partial rescue of unc-129 de-repression in DA9 of egl-5 mutants.
claims.source: Mis-expression of egl-5 in all 9 DA neurons (DA1-9) (using a fragment of the unc-4 promoter, Ex [unc-4prom::egl-5]) results in partial rescue of unc-129 de-repression in DA9 of egl-5 mutants.
claims.evidence: Demonstrated through rescue experiment shown in Figure 7B

claims.claim: Mis-expression of egl-5 in all DA neurons results in repression of unc-129 expression in anterior DA neurons (DA1-7).
claims.source: In addition, mis-expression of egl-5 in all 9 DA neurons results in repression of unc-129 expression in anterior DA neurons (DA1-7), demonstrating that EGL-5 is also sufficient to repress unc-129 expression.
claims.evidence: Demonstrated through mis-expression experiment shown in Figure 7B

claims.claim: EGL-5 is sufficient to repress unc-129 expression.
claims.source: Since EGL-5 is required for repressing unc-129 in DA9, we also performed a sufficiency experiment where we misexpressed EGL-5 in DA1-7 neurons along the VNC and indeed found that EGL-5 is sufficient to repress unc-129 expression in these neurons (Figure 7B).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated through mis-expression experiment shown in Figure 7B

claims.claim: EGL-5 acts cell autonomously.
claims.source: As the promoter (unc-4) we used to drive egl-5 expression is also expressed in DA9, we observed partial rescue of unc-129 de-repression in DA9 of egl-5 null animals, indicating that EGL-5 acts cell autonomously (Figure 7B).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated through rescue experiment shown in Figure 7B

claims.claim: EGL-5 has a dual role in DA9 and VA12 neurons: activating subclass-specific genes and repressing anterior subclass features.
claims.source: We conclude that EGL-5 has a dual role in DA9 and VA12 neurons. Apart from working together with UNC-3 to activate the expression of DA9- and VA12-specific genes (Figure 4C–E, model in Figure 5E), EGL-5 is also required to repress features associated with DA1-7 and VA1-11 neurons located more anteriorly (Figure 7A).
claims.evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing both activation and repression functions

claims.claim: lin-39 is de-repressed in DA9 and VA12 neurons in 100% of egl-5 mutant animals.
claims.source: We find no evidence for mab-5 de-repression (Figure 7—figure supplement 1), but we observed lin-39 de-repression in the DA9 and VA12 neurons in 100% of egl-5 mutant animals (Figure 7C).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated through experimental analysis shown in Figure 7C

claims.claim: The posterior Hox gene egl-5 represses the mid-body Hox gene lin-39 in DA9 and VA12 neurons.
claims.source: Consistent with these reports, our analysis demonstrates, with single-neuron resolution, that the posterior Hox gene egl-5 represses the mid-body Hox gene lin-39 in DA9 and VA12 neurons.
claims.evidence: Demonstrated through experimental analysis showing lin-39 de-repression in egl-5 mutants

claims.claim: egl-5 expression is not affected in motor neurons of lin-39 mab-5 animals.
claims.source: However, we found no differences when we monitored egl-5 expression in MNs of lin-39 mab-5 animals (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated through experimental analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1

claims.claim: Loss of egl-5 results in misplacement of DA9 neuromuscular synapses such that they are located more anteriorly in the dorsal nerve cord.
claims.source: We find that loss of egl-5 results in misplacement of the DA9 neuromuscular synapses such that they are located more anteriorly in the DNC, in a territory normally reserved for neuromuscular synapses of more anteriorly located DA neurons (Figure 8A).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated through experimental analysis shown in Figure 8A

claims.claim: EGL-5 functions cell-autonomously to control aspects of DA9 identity.
claims.source: These defects can be partially rescued by driving egl-5 expression specifically in DA9 using the glr-4 promoter which is partially affected by egl-5 (Figure 4D), indicating that EGL-5 functions cell-autonomously to control aspects of DA9 identity (Figure 8A).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated through rescue experiment shown in Figure 8A

claims.claim: In adult egl-5 mutants, the synaptic input from AVG to DA9 is lost.
claims.source: We find that in adult egl-5 mutants, this synaptic input is lost, consistent with the neuron adopting the identity of a more anterior DA neuron (Figure 8B).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated through GRASP analysis shown in Figure 8B

claims.claim: The initial establishment of the AVG to DA9 synaptic input is unaffected in egl-5 mutants.
claims.source: The initial establishment of the synaptic input is, however, unaffected (L1 stage in Figure 8B), suggesting that egl-5 controls maintenance of subclass-specific synaptic connectivity.
claims.evidence: Demonstrated through GRASP analysis at L1 stage shown in Figure 8B

claims.claim: egl-5 controls maintenance of subclass-specific synaptic connectivity.
claims.source: The initial establishment of the synaptic input is, however, unaffected (L1 stage in Figure 8B), suggesting that egl-5 controls maintenance of subclass-specific synaptic connectivity.
claims.evidence: Inferred from loss of synaptic input in adults but not at L1 stage in egl-5 mutants

claims.claim: A Hox gene controls motor neuron subclass-specific synaptic wiring patterns.
claims.source: Taken together, our analysis therefore demonstrates that a Hox gene not only controls molecular markers, but may also control MN subclass-specific synaptic wiring patterns.
claims.evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing egl-5 effects on synaptic connectivity

claims.claim: The expression of the DA1-7 marker unc-129 is de-repressed in DA8 neurons of mab-5 mutants.
claims.source: We indeed found that – similarly to the effect of EGL-5 in DA9 neurons – the expression of the DA1-7 marker unc-129 is de-repressed in DA8 neurons of mab-5 mutants (Figure 9A–B).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated through experimental analysis shown in Figure 9A–B

claims.claim: The DA9-specific markers mig-13, glr-4 and itr-1 are de-repressed in the DA8 neuron of mab-5 mutants.
claims.source: DA8 not only adopts features of the more anterior DA neurons, but, unexpectedly, it also adopts features of the more posterior DA9 neuron. Specifically, the DA9-specific markers mig-13, glr-4 and itr-1 are de-repressed in the DA8 neuron of mab-5(-) animals (Figure 9A–B)(Sym et al., 1999).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated through experimental analysis shown in Figure 9A–B and supported by citation to Sym et al., 1999

claims.claim: mab-5 binds to the cis-regulatory region of mig-13 and itr-1.
claims.source: ChIP-sequencing results from the modENCODE project demonstrate that mab-5 binds to the cis-regulatory region of mig-13 and itr-1 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), indicating that mab-5 may directly repress the expression of these DA9-specific genes in the DA8 neuron.
claims.evidence: Based on ChIP-seq data from modENCODE project shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1

claims.claim: mab-5 may directly repress the expression of DA9-specific genes in the DA8 neuron.
claims.source: ChIP-sequencing results from the modENCODE project demonstrate that mab-5 binds to the cis-regulatory region of mig-13 and itr-1 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), indicating that mab-5 may directly repress the expression of these DA9-specific genes in the DA8 neuron.
claims.evidence: Inferred from mab-5 binding to cis-regulatory regions and de-repression in mab-5 mutants

claims.claim: mab-5 ensures the adoption of DA8 fate by preventing the expression of DA1-7-specific and DA9-specific features.
claims.source: Taken together, our results show that mab-5 ensures the adoption of DA8 fate by preventing the expression of DA1-7-specific and DA9-specific features (Figure 9C).
claims.evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing de-repression of both anterior and posterior markers in mab-5 mutants

claims.claim: In the absence of mab-5, the DA8 neuron adopts a 'mixed' fate characterized by DA1-7 and DA9 traits.
claims.source: Hence, in the absence of mab-5, the DA8 neuron adopts a 'mixed' fate characterized by DA1-7 and DA9 traits.
claims.evidence: Inferred from de-repression of both DA1-7 and DA9 markers in DA8 of mab-5 mutants

claims.claim: The terminal selector unc-3 and the Hox gene mab-5 control avr-15/GluR expression in VA11 and AS11 neurons.
claims.source: We find that mab-5 is required for avr-15/GluR expression in VA11 and AS11 neurons (Figure 9D–E). unc-3 is also required for avr-15/GluR (Figure 9D–E), thereby again corroborating the theme of unc-3 cooperating with Hox genes in motor neuron subclass specification.
claims.evidence: Demonstrated through experimental analysis shown in Figure 9D–E

claims.claim: UNC-3 and HOX genes collaborate to control the expression of intermediary regulatory factors.
claims.source: The data described above indicates a direct collaboration of the UNC-3 terminal selector with Hox genes in specific motor neuron subclasses on the cis-regulatory level of 'nuts and bolts' effector genes that define specific cellular phenotypes. We also found evidence for a collaboration of UNC-3 with HOX genes in controlling the expression of intermediary regulatory factors.
claims.evidence: Demonstrated through experimental analysis in this study

claims.claim: cfi-1 is expressed in DA1-DA8 motor neurons but not in DA9.
claims.source: For example, the ARID-type transcription factor cfi-1 is expressed in the DA1-DA8 MNs, but not in DA9 (Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: Shown in Figure 1B

claims.claim: cfi-1 expression is controlled by unc-3.
claims.source: cfi-1 expression is controlled by unc-3 (Kerk et al., 2017) and we investigated the impact of HOX genes on the subclass specificity of cfi-1 expression.
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Kerk et al., 2017

claims.claim: lin-39 and mab-5 are jointly required to activate cfi-1 in DA1-DA8.
claims.source: We found that the DA9-expressed gene egl-5 is not involved in restricting cfi-1 to DA1-8, but rather lin-39 and mab-5 are jointly required to activate cfi-1 in DA1-DA8 (Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated through experimental analysis shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1

claims.claim: The ionotropic glutamate receptor glr-4 becomes derepressed in DA1-DA8 in cfi-1 mutants.
claims.source: The ionotropic glutamate receptor glr-4, normally expressed only in the SAB neurons and the DA9 subclass neuron, becomes derepressed in the remaining DA neurons (DA1-DA8) in cfi-1 mutants (Kerk et al., 2017) and, consequently, also in lin-39 mab-5 mutants (Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated through experimental analysis shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1 and supported by citation to Kerk et al., 2017

claims.claim: cfi-1 regulation by lin-39 and mab-5 is HOX gene- and cell-specific.
claims.source: cfi-1 regulation by lin-39 and mab-5 is HOX gene- and cell-specific, since the posterior HOX gene egl-5 does not affect cfi-1 expression, i.e. we observed no de-repression of cfi-1 in the DA9 neuron of egl-5 mutants (Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated through experimental analysis shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1

claims.claim: There is no cross-regulatory relationship between cfi-1 and HOX genes.
claims.source: There is no cross-regulatory relationship between cfi-1 and HOX genes, since HOX gene expression is unaffected in cfi-1 mutants (Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated through experimental analysis shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1

claims.claim: bnc-1 is expressed in all VA and VB neurons except the anterior-most VB neuron VB1.
claims.source: A similar effect of HOX genes can also be observed on the expression of another MN class-specific repressor, bnc-1. This Zn finger transcription factor is expressed in VA/VB MNs, is a direct target of UNC-3, and antagonizes the activity of UNC-3 on a number of effector genes in VA/VB (Kerk et al., 2017). bnc-1 is expressed in all VA and VB neurons, except the anterior-most VB neuron VB1.
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Kerk et al., 2017 and demonstrated through expression analysis

claims.claim: bnc-1 is a direct target of UNC-3.
claims.source: This Zn finger transcription factor is expressed in VA/VB MNs, is a direct target of UNC-3, and antagonizes the activity of UNC-3 on a number of effector genes in VA/VB (Kerk et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Kerk et al., 2017

claims.claim: bnc-1 antagonizes the activity of UNC-3 on a number of effector genes in VA/VB.
claims.source: This Zn finger transcription factor is expressed in VA/VB MNs, is a direct target of UNC-3, and antagonizes the activity of UNC-3 on a number of effector genes in VA/VB (Kerk et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Kerk et al., 2017

claims.claim: In lin-39 mab-5 mutants, bnc-1 expression is diminished in motor neurons in the midbody region.
claims.source: We indeed found that in lin-39 mab-5 mutants, bnc-1 expression is diminished in MNs in the midbody region (Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated through experimental analysis shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1

claims.claim: unc-3 and HOX genes collaborate to regulate the expression of intermediary regulatory factors.
claims.source: In conclusion, unc-3 and HOX genes collaborate not only on the regulation of terminal effector genes that define terminal cellular phenotypes, but they also collaborate to regulate the expression of intermediary regulatory factors.
claims.evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing HOX gene effects on cfi-1 and bnc-1 expression

claims.claim: An intersectional gene regulatory strategy of distinct Hox genes and a broadly-acting transcription factor generates neuronal subclass diversity.
claims.source: We provide here insights into the problem of how anatomically and functionally defined neuron classes diversify into specialized subclasses. Although the molecular mechanisms that generate interclass diversity, that is, differences between neuron classes, are beginning to be uncovered in multiple distinct systems, the mechanisms of subclass diversification have remained more elusive.
claims.evidence: Main conclusion of the study based on experimental data

claims.claim: The terminal selector UNC-3 controls features shared by all motor neuron class members and is also required for subclass diversification.
claims.source: First, we find that the terminal selector-type transcription factor UNC-3 – apart from controlling features shared by all MN class members – is also required for subclass diversification by regulating the expression of MN subclass-specific genes.
claims.evidence: Demonstrated through experimental analysis in this study

claims.claim: Three C. elegans Hox genes act synergistically and cooperate with UNC-3 in an intersectional manner to control the expression of motor neuron subclass-specific genes along the anterior-posterior axis.
claims.source: Third, we uncovered that the posterior Hox gene egl-5/Abd-B/ Hox9-Hox13, apart from acting as an UNC-3 co-activator to generate MN subclass diversity, is also required to repress the expression of the mid-body Hox gene lin-39/Scr/Dfd/Hox4-Hox5, while the Hox gene, mab-5/Antp/Hox6-Hox8, may operate as both an activator and repressor directly on its effector genes.
claims.evidence: Demonstrated through experimental analysis in this study

claims.claim: The posterior Hox gene egl-5 is required to repress the expression of the mid-body Hox gene lin-39.
claims.source: Third, we uncovered that the posterior Hox gene egl-5/Abd-B/ Hox9-Hox13, apart from acting as an UNC-3 co-activator to generate MN subclass diversity, is also required to repress the expression of the mid-body Hox gene lin-39/Scr/Dfd/Hox4-Hox5, while the Hox gene, mab-5/Antp/Hox6-Hox8, may operate as both an activator and repressor directly on its effector genes.
claims.evidence: Demonstrated through experimental analysis in this study

claims.claim: The Hox gene mab-5 may operate as both an activator and repressor directly on its effector genes.
claims.source: Third, we uncovered that the posterior Hox gene egl-5/Abd-B/ Hox9-Hox13, apart from acting as an UNC-3 co-activator to generate MN subclass diversity, is also required to repress the expression of the mid-body Hox gene lin-39/Scr/Dfd/Hox4-Hox5, while the Hox gene, mab-5/Antp/Hox6-Hox8, may operate as both an activator and repressor directly on its effector genes.
claims.evidence: Demonstrated through experimental analysis in this study

claims.claim: The intersectional activity of a single, broadly-acting terminal selector and distinct Hox genes constitutes a conceptually straightforward solution to how neuronal subclass diversity is generated along the anterior-posterior axis.
claims.source: Hence, the intersectional activity of a single, broadly-acting terminal selector and distinct Hox genes may constitute a conceptually straightforward solution to the intriguing problem of how neuronal subclass diversity is generated along the A-P axis of the nervous system.
claims.evidence: Main conclusion of the study based on experimental data

claims.claim: Diversification of distinct C. elegans motor neuron classes involves class-specific direct repression of effector genes.
claims.source: Recent work has demonstrated that diversification of distinct C. elegans MN classes (i.e. interclass diversification) involves class-specific direct repression of effector genes (Kerk et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Kerk et al., 2017

claims.claim: Motor neuron subclass diversity is mainly generated through positive regulatory inputs provided by UNC-3 and Hox proteins to subclass-specific effector genes.
claims.source: In contrast, our genetic and cis-regulatory analyses show that MN subclass diversity ("intraclass diversity") is mainly generated through positive regulatory inputs provided by UNC-3 and Hox proteins to subclass-specific effector genes (Figure 10).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated through genetic and cis-regulatory analyses in this study

claims.claim: Hox proteins can be considered as 'sub-selectors' because they selectively regulate motor neuron subclass-specific features.
claims.source: By analogy to the terminal selector function of UNC-3 that controls shared (Kratsios et al., 2015, 2011), class-specific (Kratsios et al., 2015, 2011) and subclass-specific (this study) features of MNs throughout life, Hox proteins can be considered as 'sub-selectors' because they selectively regulate MN subclass-specific features.
claims.evidence: Conceptual inference based on experimental data

claims.claim: The diversification of the SAB class of head motor neurons and ASE class of gustatory neurons in C. elegans relies on direct repression of subclass-specific effector genes.
claims.source: This regulatory principle of co-activation of subclass-specific genes is certainly not the only mechanism to achieve neuronal subclass diversity. For example, the diversification of the SAB class of head MNs and ASE class of gustatory neurons in C. elegans relies on direct repression of subclass-specific effector genes (Etchberger et al., 2009; Kerk et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Etchberger et al., 2009 and Kerk et al., 2017

claims.claim: Hox genes are required for neuronal diversity, cell survival, axonal pathfinding and circuit assembly.
claims.source: Collectively, this large body of work has established that Hox genes are required for neuronal diversity, cell survival, axonal pathfinding and circuit assembly.
claims.evidence: Based on established knowledge from multiple studies

claims.claim: Only a handful of Hox downstream targets have been identified in the nervous system to date.
claims.source: However, only a handful of Hox downstream targets have been identified in the nervous system to date and the mechanistic details of how Hox genes interact with other transcription factors during neuronal development remained ill-defined.
claims.evidence: Based on review of existing literature

claims.claim: Seven effector genes and two intermediary regulatory factors (cfi-1 and bnc-1) are Hox downstream targets.
claims.source: Our findings provide novel insights on the molecular mechanisms employed by Hox genes to control neuronal diversity: (i) by identifying seven effector genes and two intermediary regulatory factors (cfi-1 and bnc-1) as Hox downstream targets and (ii) by demonstrating that distinct Hox genes intersect with a broadly-acting, terminal selector-type transcription factor and act together at the cis-regulatory level of effector genes to generate MN subclass diversity.
claims.evidence: Demonstrated through experimental analysis in this study

claims.claim: Hox genes control the expression of motor neuron subclass-specific genes during development and may maintain effector gene expression or serve additional roles in adult life.
claims.source: Given the maintained expression of Hox genes in adult C. elegans MNs and mouse CNS (Hutlet et al., 2016), we surmise that Hox genes, apart from controlling the expression of MN subclass-specific genes during development, may also maintain effector gene expression or serve additional roles in adult life.
claims.evidence: Inferred from maintained expression of Hox genes in adults and supported by citation to Hutlet et al., 2016

claims.claim: egl-5 is required for the maintenance (not the initial formation) of the synaptic input that the DA9 motor neuron receives from AVG interneurons.
claims.source: We indeed uncovered an unexpected role for the posterior Hox gene egl-5/Abd-B/Hox9-Hox13 in adult animals, as egl-5/Abd-B/Hox9-Hox13 is required for the maintenance (not the initial formation) of the synaptic input that the DA9 MN receives from AVG interneurons.
claims.evidence: Demonstrated through GRASP analysis in this study

claims.claim: Hox genes are required for synaptic input received by motor neurons.
claims.source: Apart from adding a temporal dimension to the function of egl-5/Abd-B/Hox9-Hox13, these findings also demonstrate that Hox genes are required for synaptic input received by MNs, extending previous reports on the requirement of Hox genes for MN to muscle connectivity (Catela et al., 2015, 2016; Friedrich et al., 2016; Hessinger et al., 2017; Philippidou and Dasen, 2013).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated through experimental analysis in this study and supported by citations to Catela et al., 2015, 2016; Friedrich et al., 2016; Hessinger et al., 2017; Philippidou and Dasen, 2013

claims.claim: EGL-5 represses the expression of lin-39 in posterior touch sensory neurons in C. elegans.
claims.source: Supporting the generality of this dual mechanism of action, a recent study demonstrated a similar, dual role for EGL-5 in the diversification of posterior touch sensory neurons in C.elegans (Zheng et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Zheng et al., 2015

claims.claim: The posterior Hox genes Hoxa10, Hoxc10, and Hoxd10 in the mouse spinal cord are required for the acquisition of posterior motor neuron fate and for repression of anterior motor neuron identity.
claims.source: Moreover, the posterior Hox genes Hoxa10, Hoxc10, and Hoxd10 in the mouse spinal cord appear to function in a similar manner since they are required not only for the acquisition of posterior MN fate but also for repression of anterior MN identity (Hostikka et al., 2009; Lin and Carpenter, 2003; Wahba et al., 2001; Wu et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Hostikka et al., 2009; Lin and Carpenter, 2003; Wahba et al., 2001; Wu et al., 2008

claims.claim: Posterior Hox genes diversify posterior neurons from their more anterior counterparts.
claims.source: This dual mechanism of posterior Hox gene action may explain how neuronal subclass diversity arises from an evolutionary standpoint, i.e. posterior Hox genes diversify posterior neurons from their more anterior counterparts.
claims.evidence: Speculative inference based on experimental data

claims.claim: Homeotic transformations associated with Hox gene mutations have been proposed as a potential source of novelty at the single cell level that could contribute to the evolution of neuronal diversity.
claims.source: Supporting this possibility, homeotic transformations associated with Hox gene mutations have been proposed as a potential source of novelty at the single cell level that could contribute to the evolution of neuronal diversity (Arlotta and Hobert, 2015).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Arlotta and Hobert, 2015

claims.claim: Epidermal growth factor (EGF) signaling from a neighboring cell to the P12 neuroblast is necessary for the initiation of egl-5 expression in P12.
claims.source: The signals that initiate lin-39 and mab-5 expression in VNC MNs are not clear, but it has been shown that epidermal growth factor (EGF) signaling from a neighboring cell to the P12 neuroblast (which produces the VA12 neuron) is necessary for the initiation of egl-5 expression in P12 (Jiang and Sternberg, 1998).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Jiang and Sternberg, 1998

claims.claim: Ebf2 is co-expressed with distinct Hox genes in medial motor column (MMC) motor neurons along the anterior-posterior axis of the mouse spinal cord.
claims.source: We found that Ebf2, one of the four unc-3 mouse orthologs, is co-expressed with distinct Hox genes in medial motor column (MMC) MNs along the A-P axis of the mouse spinal cord (Figure 10—figure supplements 1 and 2), leading us to speculate that Ebf2 and Hox may work together to generate MMC subclass diversity along the A-P axis, which is perhaps essential for innervation of distinct body wall (axial) muscles.
claims.evidence: Demonstrated through expression analysis shown in Figure 10—figure supplements 1 and 2

claims.claim: Ebf2 and Hox may work together to generate MMC subclass diversity along the anterior-posterior axis.
claims.source: We found that Ebf2, one of the four unc-3 mouse orthologs, is co-expressed with distinct Hox genes in medial motor column (MMC) MNs along the A-P axis of the mouse spinal cord (Figure 10—figure supplements 1 and 2), leading us to speculate that Ebf2 and Hox may work together to generate MMC subclass diversity along the A-P axis, which is perhaps essential for innervation of distinct body wall (axial) muscles.
claims.evidence: Speculative inference based on co-expression data

claims.claim: Hox genes and the transcription factor FoxP1 are essential for diversification of spinal motor neurons of the lateral motor column (LMC) population.
claims.source: Intriguingly, Hox genes and the transcription factor, FoxP1, are essential for diversification of spinal MNs of the lateral motor column (LMC) population, although the direct downstream effector genes of FoxP1 and Hox are largely unknown (Dasen et al., 2008; Rousso et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Dasen et al., 2008 and Rousso et al., 2008

claims.claim: The expression of distinct Hox genes intersects with the broadly-acting transcription factor Pet-1 in molecularly and functionally distinct populations of serotonergic neurons in the mouse brainstem.
claims.source: Moving beyond MNs, a recent study on the molecular deconstruction of the serotonergic system in the mouse brainstem has revealed that the expression of distinct Hox genes intersects with the broadly-acting transcription factor Pet-1 in molecularly and functionally distinct populations of serotonergic neurons (Okaty et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Okaty et al., 2015

claims.claim: The intersectional gene regulatory principle may be utilized for the fractionation of neuronal classes into subclasses.
claims.source: We propose that this intersectional gene regulatory principle may be utilized for the fractionation of neuronal classes into subclasses.
claims.evidence: Proposed based on findings in this study and other systems

claims.claim: Fractionation of neuronal classes into subclasses is essential for the acquisition of subclass-specific traits, which could ultimately lead to the evolution of novel neuron types and circuits.
claims.source: Such fractionation is essential for the acquisition of subclass-specific traits, which could ultimately lead to the evolution of novel neuron types and circuits.
claims.evidence: Speculative inference about evolutionary implications

results.result: C. elegans motor neurons are organized into seven anatomically distinct classes (DA, DB, SAB, AS, VA, VB, VC) defined by unique morphology, axodendritic projection patterns, synaptic connectivity, and class-specific expression of effector genes including neurotransmitter receptors, ion channels, gap junction proteins, and signaling molecules.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C6 are well-supported by multiple citations to established literature (White et al., 1986; Hobert et al., 2016; Von Stetina et al., 2006) and are corroborated by Figure 1A-B showing anatomical organization and molecular markers. These represent foundational anatomical and molecular characterization of the system under study.

results.result: Motor neuron subclasses within each class display position-dependent differences in synaptic connectivity along the anterior-posterior axis, with posterior-most neurons (e.g., DA8, DA9) receiving selective input from tail sensory neurons, enabling integration of head and tail information.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C8, C12-C14 are supported by connectivity data from the C. elegans wiring diagram (Figure 1B, Figure 1—source data 1, www.wormwiring.org) and citations to White et al., 1986. The functional interpretation in C14 is reasonable inference from the connectivity patterns, though direct functional validation is not provided.

results.result: The genes unc-4 and unc-37 are selectively required in VA neurons located in the VNC (VA2-VA10) but not in the retrovesicular ganglion (VA1) or preanal ganglion (VA11, VA12) to specify correct presynaptic input patterns.
results.evaluation: Claim C9 is supported by multiple citations (Miller et al., 1992; Pflugrad et al., 1997; White et al., 1992) describing prior genetic studies. This represents established knowledge about region-specific gene function in motor neuron specification.

results.result: Subclass-specific molecular markers distinguish motor neuron subclasses: unc-129/TGFβ is expressed in DA1-7 but not DA8-DA9, while itr-1 is exclusively expressed in DA9.
results.evaluation: Claims C10-C11 are supported by citations (Colavita et al., 1998; Klassen and Shen, 2007) and Figure 1B showing expression patterns. These markers provide molecular evidence for subclass diversity and are used throughout the study.

results.result: Sexual dimorphisms exist in motor neuron connectivity: 68 male-specific neurons in the tail make extensive connections with posterior-most motor neurons, and sex-shared neurons show sexually dimorphic connectivity patterns (e.g., AVG innervates DA9 only in males, PHB innervates VA12 only in hermaphrodites).
results.evaluation: Claims C15-C19 are supported by citations (Sulston et al., 1980; Jarrell et al., 2012; White et al., 1986) and connectivity data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—source data 1. This establishes the biological relevance of subclass diversity in the context of sexual dimorphism.

results.result: The terminal selector transcription factor UNC-3 controls both class-specific features shared by all motor neuron class members and subclass-specific features, with its activity counteracted by class-specific repressor proteins to generate interclass diversity.
results.evaluation: Claims C20-C22 are supported by prior work (Kratsios et al., 2015, 2011; Kerk et al., 2017) and experimental data in this study. C21 represents a novel finding of this manuscript, while C20 and C22 represent established knowledge that provides context.

results.result: Several motor neuron-expressed genes (rig-4, acr-2, acr-5, acr-16, unc-53) are expressed in all individual members of a given motor neuron class, confirming class-level molecular identity.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C26 are supported by expression analysis in this study. C26 represents established orthology knowledge. These class-specific markers validate the classification system and contrast with subclass-specific markers.

results.result: UNC-3 directly regulates subclass-specific genes (mig-13, itr-1, glr-4 in DA9; unc-129 in DA1-7) through COE motifs in their cis-regulatory regions, as demonstrated by mutational analysis showing COE motifs are essential for expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C31 are strongly supported by experimental data in Figure 2A-E, including expression analysis in unc-3 mutants, bioinformatic identification of COE motifs, and cis-regulatory reporter assays with motif mutations. This provides direct mechanistic evidence for UNC-3 function in subclass specification.

results.result: UNC-3 directly controls subclass-specific gene expression in VA neurons (mig-13 and flp-18 in VA12; del-1 in VA1-VA11) and AS neurons (avr-15 in AS11), with COE motifs overrepresented in cis-regulatory regions of these genes.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C36 are supported by experimental data in Figure 2B-C and Table 1, including expression analysis in unc-3 mutants and cis-regulatory analysis. This extends the UNC-3 regulatory mechanism to multiple motor neuron classes.

results.result: unc-3 is expressed in all nine neurons of the DA class and all twelve neurons of the VA class.
results.evaluation: Claim C37 is supported by citations to Kratsios et al., 2011 and Pereira et al., 2015. This establishes the paradox that motivates the search for region-specific cofactors: if UNC-3 is expressed in all class members, why are subclass-specific genes only expressed in subsets?

results.result: Three C. elegans Hox genes (lin-39, mab-5, egl-5) are differentially expressed in motor neuron subclasses along the anterior-posterior axis: egl-5 in DA9 and VA12, mab-5 in DA8 and AS11, and lin-39/mab-5 co-expression in more anterior neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C46 are strongly supported by fosmid-based reporter expression analysis shown in Figure 3A-D. The use of fosmid reporters (containing ~30 kb genomic regions) provides high confidence in expression patterns. This establishes the spatial code of Hox gene expression that underlies the intersectional mechanism.

results.result: Hox mutants show normal motor neuron number and maintain expression of pan-neuronal markers and shared cholinergic genes, indicating Hox genes are not required for motor neuron generation or basic cholinergic identity.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C48 are supported by experimental data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and citation to Stefanakis et al., 2015. This important control demonstrates that Hox genes specifically affect subclass identity rather than general motor neuron specification or survival.

results.result: lin-39 and mab-5 function redundantly to control unc-129 expression in DA1-7 neurons: single mutants show mild or no effects, but lin-39 mab-5 double mutants and ceh-20/PBX mutants show profound effects.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C54 are supported by experimental data in Figure 4A and citations establishing ceh-20 as the C. elegans PBX homolog and Hox cofactor. The genetic redundancy analysis is rigorous, and the PBX requirement supports a canonical Hox-PBX mechanism.

results.result: EGL-5 controls DA9-specific genes (itr-1, glr-4, mig-13) with effects milder than unc-3 mutants, and functions independently of CEH-20/PBX, consistent with Abd-B proteins functioning without PBX cofactors.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C58 are supported by experimental data in Figure 4C-E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1, with citations supporting PBX-independent Abd-B function. The milder effects compared to unc-3 suggest partial redundancy or additional factors, which is appropriately noted.

results.result: egl-5 controls VA12-specific genes (mig-13, flp-18), while lin-39/mab-5 and ceh-20/PBX control del-1 expression in VA1-VA11 neurons, with del-1 under direct UNC-3 control.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C62 are supported by experimental data in Figure 4B-E. This extends the Hox regulatory mechanism to the VA class and demonstrates both anterior (lin-39/mab-5) and posterior (egl-5) Hox genes control distinct subclass-specific genes.

results.result: Hox genes (lin-39, mab-5, egl-5) are expressed in post-mitotic motor neurons into adulthood, suggesting continuous cell-autonomous control of subclass features, with LIN-39 maintaining its own expression through positive autoregulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C66 are supported by expression data in Figure 3B-C and citation to Niu et al., 2011 for LIN-39 autoregulation. C64 is appropriately qualified as a suggestion. The persistent expression supports a maintenance function but does not prove it—this would require temporal inactivation experiments.

results.result: UNC-3 and Hox proteins act in parallel pathways: Hox gene expression is unaffected in unc-3 mutants, unc-3 expression is unaffected in egl-5 mutants, and Hox genes do not affect ACh pathway genes (direct UNC-3 targets).
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C71 are supported by experimental data in Figure 5A-B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1. The lack of cross-regulation is important evidence for parallel rather than hierarchical pathways. C69 is appropriately qualified as a suggestion based on the data.

results.result: unc-3(fp8); lin-39 mab-5 triple mutants show stronger effects on unc-129 and del-1 expression than double or single mutants, demonstrating UNC-3 and Hox factors act synergistically to generate subclass diversity.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C73 are supported by experimental data in Figure 5C-D using a hypomorphic unc-3 allele. The additive genetic effects combined with lack of cross-regulation provide strong evidence for synergistic action. The use of a hypomorphic allele is appropriate to avoid ceiling effects.

results.result: LIN-39 directly controls unc-129 and del-1 expression through discrete GATTGATG binding sites: mutation of LIN-39 sites causes dramatic loss of reporter expression, and ChIP-seq data show LIN-39 and MAB-5 binding to these regions.
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C79 are strongly supported by bioinformatic analysis, cis-regulatory reporter assays with site-directed mutagenesis (Figure 6B-F), and ChIP-seq data from modENCODE (Figure 6—figure supplement 1). This provides direct mechanistic evidence for Hox protein binding and function at target genes.

results.result: EGL-5 has a dual role in DA9 and VA12: it activates posterior-specific genes (with UNC-3) and represses anterior markers (unc-129, del-1), with egl-5 mutants showing de-repression of anterior markers and mis-expression rescuing/repressing unc-129 in a cell-autonomous manner.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C87 are strongly supported by loss-of-function analysis (Figure 7A), gain-of-function/rescue experiments (Figure 7B), and cell-autonomous rescue. The dual activation/repression function is well-demonstrated through complementary genetic approaches. This represents a key mechanistic insight into how posterior Hox genes establish identity.

results.result: The posterior Hox gene egl-5 represses the mid-body Hox gene lin-39 in DA9 and VA12 neurons: lin-39 is de-repressed in 100% of egl-5 mutants in these neurons, but egl-5 expression is unaffected in lin-39 mab-5 mutants.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C90 are supported by expression analysis in Figure 7C and Figure 7—figure supplement 1. This demonstrates posterior dominance/Hox cross-regulation at single-neuron resolution. The unidirectional regulation (egl-5 represses lin-39 but not vice versa) is consistent with canonical Hox posterior prevalence.

results.result: Loss of egl-5 causes anterior misplacement of DA9 neuromuscular synapses in the dorsal nerve cord, and this defect is partially rescued by cell-autonomous egl-5 expression in DA9.
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C92 are supported by synaptic localization analysis in Figure 8A using presynaptic markers and cell-autonomous rescue. The quantification uses seam cells as anatomical landmarks. The partial rescue is appropriately noted and may reflect partial effectiveness of the glr-4 promoter (which is itself partially egl-5-dependent).

results.result: egl-5 controls maintenance (not initial establishment) of the male-specific AVG to DA9 synaptic input: the synapse forms normally at L1 stage but is lost in adult egl-5 mutants, demonstrating Hox control of subclass-specific synaptic wiring.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C96 are strongly supported by GRASP analysis at L1 and adult stages in Figure 8B. The temporal analysis distinguishing formation from maintenance is rigorous and represents an important finding about Hox function in circuit maintenance. C95-C96 are appropriately qualified as inferences.

results.result: mab-5 ensures DA8 fate by repressing both anterior (DA1-7) and posterior (DA9) features: in mab-5 mutants, DA8 adopts a mixed fate with de-repression of unc-129 (DA1-7 marker) and DA9-specific markers (mig-13, glr-4, itr-1), with ChIP-seq showing mab-5 binding to DA9 marker genes.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C102 are supported by expression analysis in Figure 9A-B and ChIP-seq data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1. The mixed fate phenotype is unexpected and interesting, showing mab-5 functions differently than egl-5. C100 is appropriately qualified as inference, though the ChIP-seq data provide strong support for direct repression.

results.result: Both unc-3 and mab-5 control avr-15/GluR expression in VA11 and AS11 neurons, corroborating the theme of unc-3 cooperating with Hox genes in motor neuron subclass specification.
results.evaluation: Claim C103 is supported by experimental data in Figure 9D-E. This extends the UNC-3/Hox cooperation mechanism to another subclass marker and motor neuron class (AS), strengthening the generality of the intersectional mechanism.

results.result: UNC-3 and Hox genes collaborate to control intermediary regulatory factors: lin-39 and mab-5 jointly activate cfi-1 in DA1-DA8 (but not egl-5), and loss of cfi-1 or lin-39/mab-5 causes de-repression of glr-4 in DA1-DA8, with no cross-regulation between cfi-1 and Hox genes.
results.evaluation: Claims C104-C110 are supported by expression analysis in Figure 9—figure supplement 1 and citations to Kerk et al., 2017. This demonstrates the intersectional mechanism operates at multiple levels of the regulatory hierarchy, not just terminal effector genes. The cell-specificity and lack of cross-regulation are well-documented.

results.result: UNC-3 and Hox genes collaborate to regulate bnc-1 expression: bnc-1 is a direct UNC-3 target that antagonizes UNC-3 activity in VA/VB neurons, and its expression is diminished in lin-39 mab-5 mutants in midbody motor neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C111-C115 are supported by expression analysis in Figure 9—figure supplement 1 and citations to Kerk et al., 2017. This provides another example of Hox genes controlling intermediary regulatory factors, further demonstrating the multi-level nature of the intersectional regulatory mechanism.

results.result: An intersectional gene regulatory strategy of distinct Hox genes and the broadly-acting terminal selector UNC-3 generates motor neuron subclass diversity along the anterior-posterior axis, providing a conceptually straightforward solution to subclass diversification.
results.evaluation: Claims C116-C118, C121 represent the main conclusions of the study, synthesizing results from multiple experiments. These are well-supported by the collective evidence showing: (1) UNC-3 controls both class and subclass features, (2) Hox genes are expressed in subclass-specific patterns, (3) UNC-3 and Hox act synergistically without cross-regulation, and (4) both factors directly bind subclass-specific gene regulatory regions.

results.result: The posterior Hox gene egl-5 represses the mid-body Hox gene lin-39, while mab-5 may operate as both activator and repressor directly on its effector genes.
results.evaluation: Claims C119-C120 are supported by experimental data showing lin-39 de-repression in egl-5 mutants (Figure 7C) and mab-5 effects on both anterior and posterior markers (Figure 9A-B) with ChIP-seq evidence for direct binding. C120 is appropriately qualified as "may operate" given the mixed activation/repression phenotype.

results.result: Motor neuron subclass diversity is generated through positive regulatory inputs from UNC-3 and Hox proteins (unlike interclass diversity which involves repression), with Hox proteins functioning as 'sub-selectors' that selectively regulate subclass-specific features.
results.evaluation: Claims C122-C124 are supported by genetic and cis-regulatory analyses throughout the study (Figures 2-6) and contrast with prior work on interclass diversity (Kerk et al., 2017). The 'sub-selector' concept is a reasonable conceptual framework based on the data, though C124 represents interpretive inference rather than direct demonstration.

results.result: The diversification of SAB head motor neurons and ASE gustatory neurons in C. elegans relies on direct repression of subclass-specific effector genes, representing an alternative mechanism to the co-activation strategy.
results.evaluation: Claim C125 is supported by citations to Etchberger et al., 2009 and Kerk et al., 2017. This appropriately acknowledges that the co-activation mechanism described in this study is not universal, and other mechanisms exist for generating neuronal subclass diversity.

results.result: This study identifies seven effector genes and two intermediary regulatory factors (cfi-1, bnc-1) as Hox downstream targets in the nervous system, addressing the gap in knowledge about Hox targets and mechanisms in neuronal development.
results.evaluation: Claims C126-C128 are supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript and appropriately contextualize the contribution relative to existing knowledge. C126 represents established knowledge, C127 identifies the gap, and C128 describes the novel contribution of identifying specific Hox targets.

results.result: Hox genes control motor neuron subclass-specific gene expression during development and maintain it in adults, with egl-5 specifically required for maintenance (not formation) of synaptic inputs, extending Hox function beyond motor-to-muscle connectivity.
results.evaluation: Claims C129-C131 are supported by persistent Hox expression into adulthood (Figure 3B-C), temporal GRASP analysis (Figure 8B), and citations to prior work on motor-to-muscle connectivity. C129 is appropriately qualified as inference ("may also maintain"), while C130-C131 provide direct evidence for maintenance function.

results.result: The dual activation/repression mechanism of posterior Hox genes (activating posterior features while repressing anterior features) is conserved across systems and may explain evolutionary diversification of posterior neurons, with homeotic transformations potentially contributing to neuronal diversity evolution.
results.evaluation: Claims C132-C135 are supported by citations to studies in C. elegans touch neurons (Zheng et al., 2015) and mouse spinal cord (multiple citations). C134-C135 represent speculative evolutionary interpretations appropriately qualified as "may explain" and "potential source," supported by citation to Arlotta and Hobert, 2015.

results.result: EGF signaling from a neighboring cell to the P12 neuroblast is necessary for initiating egl-5 expression in P12 (which produces VA12), representing an intercellular signaling mechanism for diversifying posterior neuroblasts.
results.evaluation: Claim C136 is supported by citation to Jiang and Sternberg, 1998. This provides context for upstream regulation of Hox genes, though the authors appropriately note that signals initiating lin-39 and mab-5 expression in VNC motor neurons remain unclear.

results.result: Ebf2 (a unc-3 mouse ortholog) is co-expressed with distinct Hox genes in medial motor column (MMC) motor neurons along the anterior-posterior axis of the mouse spinal cord, suggesting Ebf2 and Hox may work together to generate MMC subclass diversity.
results.evaluation: Claims C137-C138 are supported by expression analysis in Figure 10—figure supplements 1-2 showing Ebf2 and Hox co-expression in mouse MMC neurons. C138 is appropriately qualified as speculation ("leading us to speculate"). This provides evidence for potential conservation of the intersectional mechanism in mammals, though functional validation would be required.

results.result: The intersectional gene regulatory principle of Hox genes with broadly-acting transcription factors (FoxP1 in LMC, Pet-1 in serotonergic neurons) may be utilized for fractionating neuronal classes into subclasses, essential for acquiring subclass-specific traits and potentially contributing to evolution of novel neuron types.
results.evaluation: Claims C139-C142 are supported by citations to studies in mouse spinal cord (Dasen et al., 2008; Rousso et al., 2008) and brainstem serotonergic neurons (Okaty et al., 2015). C141-C142 represent broader proposals appropriately qualified as speculation about general principles and evolutionary implications.
